strengths: The post-hoc use of forest partitions and neural activation patterns has an identifiable audience in uncertainty estimation. Addressing both model families without requiring OOD training examples is a useful contribution. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b10/review-experiment-wn29a6vb/call-19d7ed7d958f447baaf177775a3293d2/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical coverage is substantial: six simulations, 45 OpenML datasets, and vision experiments using two encoders. Known-posterior simulations, comparisons of Euclidean and partition-based distances, and individual dataset results provide useful evidence.

The reported tradeoffs are promising. In Table 1, KDN reduces CIFAR-100 OCE from 0.47 to 0.12 while CIFAR-10 accuracy changes from 98.06% to 97.45%. These results support further interest in the approach.

The Gaussian decay plus positive common background has a valid, understandable limiting property: for a fixed fitted model, predictions approach the empirical class priors as distance in the modeled space diverges.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central calibration claims exceed what the target and metrics establish. Equation (1) defines reversion to training priors outside a high-density region; this is a confidence convention, not generally the true posterior under distribution shift. Equation (18) compares only maximum probabilities: priors (0.9, 0.1) and predictions (0.1, 0.9) give zero OCE despite disagreeing completely about the favored class. The paper should distinguish prior reversion from probabilistic calibration and either narrow its claims or provide evidence under explicitly specified shifted distributions.

Necessary: Proposition 2 establishes only an infinite-distance limit, not calibration throughout the OOD region or attainment of Equation (1) at finite distances. In the vision experiments, Gaussians operate on encoder embeddings; distance from training images need not imply distance from their embeddings. The manuscript should explicitly restrict the guarantee to the modeled feature space and distinguish it from the empirical findings on semantic shifts.

Necessary: The probabilistic motivation needs correction. Equation (3) identifies piecewise-affine discriminative outputs with class-conditional densities, although neural logits can be negative and forest leaf probabilities are posterior estimates. Moreover, adding a positive constant throughout R^D gives nonintegrable functions. Equation (7) can still define valid normalized class scores, but that does not establish the claimed class-conditional density interpretation.

Necessary: Important experimental details are missing, including the search range and selection objective for k, the vision classification head and training settings, OE's outlier source, ACET/ODIN settings, and the numbers of repetitions and meanings of uncertainty bands. Table 1 also rounds several calibration estimates and uncertainties to 0.00, limiting interpretation of small differences. Appendix C specifies identical Gaussian mixtures for both XOR classes, contradicting the illustrated task. These issues prevent sufficiently confident assessment and reproduction of the comparisons; the promised future code release does not resolve them in the supplied manuscript.

Optional improvements: Ablations of the background term, neighboring-polytope weighting, and nearest-kernel selection would clarify which components produce the gains. Reliability diagrams or proper scoring rules would strengthen the ID analysis. Detection metrics would help evaluate ODIN on its intended ranking task, while runtime and memory measurements would clarify practical scalability.
